## Problem 1: Shared birthdays

The `shared_bday` function below randomly samples $n$ birthdays from 365 equally 
likely days and returns `TRUE` if at least one birthday is repeated.

```{r bday-function}
shared_bday = function(n) {
  bdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  repeated_bday = length(unique(bdays)) < n
  return(repeated_bday)
}
```

Next, I run the function 10,000 times for each group size from 2 to 50 and 
average the results to estimate the probability of a shared birthday.

```{r bday-sim}
set.seed(1118)

bday_sim =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50, 
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(group_size, shared_bday))

bday_results =
  bday_sim |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated))
```

```{r bday-plot}
bday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_of_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Simulated probability that at least two people share a birthday",
    x = "Group size (number of people)",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday",
    caption = "Based on 10,000 simulated groups per group size"
  )
```

The probability of a shared birthday rises quickly and non-linearly with group 
size. It is near zero for very small groups (`r pull(filter(bday_results, group_size == 2), prob_of_repeat)` with 2 people), crosses 0.5 at a group size of `r bday_results |> filter(prob_of_repeat >= 0.5) |> pull(group_size) |> min()`, and reaches `r pull(filter(bday_results, group_size == 50), prob_of_repeat)` with 50 people. 

## Problem 2: Longitudinal study

### Import data
```{r study-import}
study_files =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files("data/")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    path = str_c("data/", file_name),
    data = map(path, read_csv)
  )
```

### Tidy data
```{r study-tidy}
study_df =
  study_files |>
  mutate(file_name = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")) |>
  separate(file_name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    participant = str_c(arm, subject_id, sep = "-"),
    arm = case_match(
      arm,
      "con" ~ "Control",
      "exp" ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental")),
    subject_id = as.numeric(subject_id)
  ) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |>
  select(-path)
```

### Spaghetti plot
```{r spaghetti-plot}
study_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = participant, color = arm)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations for each subject, by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study arm"
  )
```

At week 1, the two arms look similar, with overlapping values. The experimental arm generally shows increasing observations over time, whereas the control arm fluctuates without a consistent upward trend. Over the 8 weeks, subjects in the experimental arm generally show increasing observations over time, while control subjects stay roughly flat around their starting level but fluctuate week to week. At week 8, every experimental subject has a higher observation than every control subject. There is variation between participants and from week to week within each arm, but the groups separate more clearly over time. This divergence between groups could suggest an effect of the experimental condition.

## Problem 3: Power of a one-sample t-test

### Simulate samples and tests

The `t_test_sim` function below generates a dataset of size $n = 30$ from a Normal distribution with $\sigma = 5$. The function then performs a one sample t-test of $H_0: \mu = 0$ and extracts the sample mean and p-value.

```{r t-test-function}
t_test_sim = function(mu) {
  sample_data = rnorm(n = 30, mean = mu, sd = 5)

  t_test_result = 
    t.test(sample_data, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
  
  return(t_test_result)
}
```

```{r sim-results}
set.seed(1118)

sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(results = map(true_mu, t_test_sim)) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  mutate(reject = p_value < 0.05)
```

```{r power_results}
power_results =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject),
    avg_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat),
    avg_mu_hat_rejected = mean(mu_hat[reject])
  )

power_results |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
